title: Blind prediction of multiphase reservoir flow

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a theory and modeling method that predicts how oil, water and gas will move through a reservoir before observing the production response being predicted. It would connect measurements of pore geometry, wettability—the tendency of fluids to contact rock surfaces—and fluid properties to field-scale forecasts of breakthrough time, oil-rate trajectories and recovery. The target is reliable prediction within declared, decision-relevant uncertainty, rather than exact knowledge of every fluid interface.

Two linked advances are needed: constitutive closure, which specifies how unresolved rock–fluid interactions affect flow, and upscaling, which carries that description from pores and laboratory samples to reservoir simulation cells. Existing extended multiphase Darcy descriptions use quantities such as relative permeability and capillary pressure to represent interactions that are not resolved explicitly. The reviewed Darcy paper describes these closures as dependent on scale and flow history, and explains that averaging can discard interface geometry, topology and connectivity.

Blind prediction also requires a clear information boundary. History matching uses observed reservoir behavior to estimate model variables; a successful match therefore answers a different question from predicting an unseen response. PET-01 seeks forecasts made without fitting or selecting the model against the target production history. Its strongest form would use rock, fluid and reservoir measurements alone, with no production-response calibration.

significance.text: If demonstrated across materially different reservoirs, this capability would make development decisions less dependent on learning the target flood's behavior after production has begun. Forecasts of when injected water or gas will arrive, how oil rates will evolve and how much oil can ultimately be recovered could inform well placement, injection schedules and comparisons among development plans. These are conditional consequences of the proposed capability, not outcomes demonstrated by the supplied papers.

The practical motivation includes the effort required for calibration. Oliver and Chen describe history matching as an inverse problem and state that obtaining even one history-matched reservoir model requires substantial work. A reliable blind forecast could reduce dependence on that retrospective fitting. However, improving constitutive closure alone would not fix field outcomes: reservoir geometry, connectivity, initial conditions, operating schedules and the assumptions used to define an economic recovery endpoint would still constrain the forecast.

An illustrative calculation explains why several moderate limitations can compound: four independent multiplicative efficiencies of 80 percent give 0.8⁴ = 40.96 percent overall efficiency. The research attributes such an example to Muggeridge and colleagues, using microscopic displacement, sweep, connected volume and economic life as the factors. The supplied review could not verify that attribution, the factor definitions or their assumptions because the source text was not captured. The arithmetic is valid, but treating those particular factors as independent multipliers remains an illustrative assumption here.

Better prediction would not itself mobilize stranded oil or guarantee higher recovery. Additional recovery would require effective physical interventions, and its value would depend on operating and economic conditions. PET-01 is therefore a predictive capability that could support the separate recovery innovations in the roster. Its significance does not require a claim of perfect simulation or a universal forecast-error threshold.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved target is a transferable connection between pore-scale rock–fluid physics and decision-relevant reservoir forecasts, with quantified uncertainty and without fitting the response being predicted. The reviewed Darcy paper identifies scale- and history-dependent uncertainty in relative permeability, capillary pressure and wettability. It also describes effective permeability as a coupled rock–fluid property, complicating any treatment of it as a fixed property of the rock alone.

Concrete barriers arise when interface physics and reservoir structure are reduced to simulation inputs. Pore-scale averaging removes explicit interface geometry and topology; capillary-pressure and contact-angle measurements may describe scales different from the simulation grid; and grid upscaling can erase connectivity and interface effects. A successful method would need to preserve the effects that control flow while remaining computationally usable at field scale. A constitutive curve measured on a core cannot, by itself, specify the reservoir's larger-scale connectivity.

A further challenge is separating uncertainty in the flow law from uncertainty in reservoir characterization. A forecast can fail because its closure is inadequate, because important flow paths were not measured, or because initial conditions and operations were specified incorrectly. As a synthesis, the breakthrough would need both an adequate physical description and sufficiently informative inputs, together with a way to propagate their uncertainty into the forecast. The supplied evidence does not establish that flood-derived curves are universally non-unique or that heterogeneity always dominates other sweep mechanisms.

current_state.text: Oliver and Chen's review was published online in 2010 and appeared in a 2011 issue of Computational Geosciences. Its accessible abstract documents reservoir history matching, methodological progress involving geostatistics and Monte Carlo methods, and attention to uncertainty quantification. The retained material available to the supplied review contained the abstract and references, not the article body. It supports the distinction between fitting observed behavior and forecasting withheld behavior, but does not establish the stronger claim that ensemble and optimization methods necessarily preserve non-uniqueness in every application.

The supplied review reports a full four-page PDF of Where Extended Darcy Models Lose Physical Fidelity in Multiphase Petroleum Flow, correcting the earlier research's description of abstract-only access. The paper describes unresolved interfaces, scale-dependent closures, possible mismatch between measurement and simulation scales, and loss of connectivity through upscaling. It is a conceptual review and explicitly offers no replacement constitutive model, so it documents modeling concerns rather than demonstrating the proposed blind-prediction capability.

That Darcy paper has an unresolved bibliographic date discrepancy: its landing page reports publication on August 12, 2026, while the PDF identifies itself as Sci Proc 2025;12:e1400 and records acceptance in August 2025. Both dates must be retained until reconciled. The supplied evidence does not justify using an assessment of venue prestige to strengthen or dismiss its technical claims.

The research attributes recovery factors of approximately 20–40 percent for mature oil-field waterfloods, 80–90 percent for gas fields, and 50–70 percent for some oil fields using combined improved- and enhanced-oil-recovery methods to Muggeridge and colleagues' 2014 paper. No source artifact was retained for the supplied review, so these ranges, their populations and their operating assumptions remain unverified in this record. They should be read as historical figures reported by the research, not as verified contemporary benchmarks or evidence that PET-01 has been achieved.

The supplied evidence establishes dated discussions of calibration and modeling limitations, but contains no demonstrated blind field-scale result sufficient to establish completion of PET-01. It also does not establish that successful blind forecasting is absent throughout petroleum engineering as of November 1, 2026: the supplied freshness record is empty. The defensible conclusion is that the proposed capability is not demonstrated by these inputs; the broader contemporary state remains unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: before observing the target production or flood response, register forecasts of breakthrough time, the oil-rate trajectory and ultimate recovery using only information available at a declared cutoff. Specify the model and its selection procedure before releasing the withheld subsequent history. A history match of those validation observations would not count as a blind prediction.
completion_criteria.label: Blind production forecasts registered before observing the target response

completion_criteria.text: For a new flood in an already producing field, state explicitly whether earlier production data may be used. Allowing them would test prediction of an unseen intervention response with prior calibration. Testing the stronger claim of prediction from rock, fluid and reservoir measurements alone would require excluding earlier production data from calibration and model selection. These two demonstrations should be reported separately because they establish different capabilities.
completion_criteria.label: Prediction capabilities distinguished by declared use of earlier production

completion_criteria.text: Declare operating schedules, initial-state assumptions, forecast uncertainty, error measures and acceptance tolerances in advance. Define ultimate recovery using an explicit physical or economic endpoint. If the full endpoint has not been observed, report recovery validation as incomplete rather than treating an extrapolation as an observed outcome. Choose proposed tolerances so that the development decision would remain unchanged across the accepted range; no numerical threshold, including 5 percent, is asserted as an industry rule.
completion_criteria.label: Decision-relevant validation criteria and recovery endpoints declared in advance

completion_criteria.text: Test more than one materially different reservoir type, including a carbonate, and document how the method handles differences in wettability, heterogeneity, connectivity and flow history. For reproducibility, provide enough measurement, preprocessing, model and operating information for independent teams to repeat the forecasts and scoring. Report failures, sensitivity to uncertain inputs and computational requirements alongside successful cases. Such finite demonstrations would establish breadth within tested conditions, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible forecasts across materially different reservoir types, including a carbonate

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: PET-02, Conventional-oil recovery at gas-field recovery factors, concerns physically achieving high recovery. PET-05, Shale-oil recovery from the matrix, and PET-09, Bitumen that flows at native reservoir temperature, concern mobilization in particular resource settings. PET-01 could help predict and compare interventions for these goals, but accurate prediction would not itself supply the required displacement, transport or viscosity-changing mechanism. Only their titles and the research's scope descriptions were supplied, so their detailed boundaries remain unverified.

Roster-based overlap: PET-08, Permeability and saturation measured through the reservoir volume, addresses information that could improve PET-01's inputs. Better measurements could reduce uncertainty in connectivity and fluid distribution, while PET-01 would still need a reliable relation between those measurements and subsequent multiphase flow. PET-10, A pressure plan with a prospectively tested earthquake bound, shares the emphasis on prospective validation, but its stated outcome concerns seismic response to pressure management rather than production forecasting.

Roster-based distinction: PET-03, Commercial gas production from methane hydrate; PET-04, Industrial in-situ conversion of oil-shale kerogen; PET-06, Hydrogen from petroleum reservoirs, with the other products left underground; and PET-11, In-reservoir conversion of bitumen to pipeline-specification crude, concern production or conversion processes. Multiphase-flow prediction could support their design, but their titles imply additional process-specific capabilities that PET-01 does not establish. PET-07, Deep well construction without a steep depth penalty, concerns access and construction economics rather than predictive flow closure. These are conceptual comparisons from the supplied roster, not assessments of those entries' technical evidence.

The research intends PET-01 to carry forward a historical 'perfect simulator' concept without an invented 5 percent forecast-error requirement. That historical entry was not supplied, so exact identity cannot be confirmed. PET-01 remains one predictive capability here; changing an error threshold alone would not justify creating a separate innovation.

change_log.reason: The review supports the technical motivation but does not establish a field-wide absence of successful forecasting or justify an exact-prediction claim.

change_log.change: Integrated interface geometry, topology, connectivity loss, history dependence and possible measurement-to-grid scale mismatch into the technical explanation.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why laboratory measurements and continuum closures may not transfer directly to field-scale forecasts.

change_log.change: Qualified universal non-uniqueness and heterogeneity-dominance assertions, and separated constitutive uncertainty from characterization and operating uncertainty.
change_log.reason: The inspected sources do not support those generalizations or show that closure alone determines field outcomes.

change_log.reason: The supplied review inspected a full PDF and identified a bibliographic discrepancy that remains unresolved.

change_log.reason: These details make the proposed demonstration assessable while preserving its status as a proposal and avoiding claims of universality from finite tests.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the field-wide availability or absence of blind, decision-relevant reservoir forecasting as of November 1, 2026; the freshness record is empty.
The Darcy paper's 2026 landing-page publication date and 2025 PDF citation and acceptance information remain unreconciled.
The Muggeridge recovery ranges, efficiency-factor definitions and attributed 41 percent example cannot be verified from the retained materials.
The extent and practical consequences of non-uniqueness in flood-derived constitutive curves are not established by the accessible Oliver and Chen abstract.
The claim that reservoir heterogeneity generally dominates viscous fingering or other sweep mechanisms remains unverified in the supplied evidence.
Exact overlap with the historical 'perfect simulator' entry and detailed boundaries of the other roster entries require their full records.
Decision-relevant tolerances, reservoir coverage and recovery endpoints remain choices to be specified for a concrete demonstration; no universal numerical completion threshold is established.

brief.title: Predicting how oil, water and gas move underground
possible: Reservoir engineers could predict when injected water or gas will reach a well, how oil output will change and how much oil can ultimately be recovered—before seeing the production response they are forecasting.

The forecasts would connect measurements of tiny spaces in rock, fluid properties and how fluids contact rock surfaces to flow across a whole reservoir. They would include uncertainty small enough to guide development decisions.
why: Operators could use these forecasts to choose well locations, plan injection schedules and compare development plans. They could depend less on adjusting models to match production after it has begun.

sources.showed: This review examines oil recovery rates, methods for increasing recovery and technological limits.
sources.cited_for: It provides context on the limits to oil recovery.
sources.not_established: It does not establish reliable reservoir forecasts made without fitting the production response being predicted.

sources.who: Dean S. Oliver and Yan Chen
sources.showed: Their review describes progress in history matching, which adjusts reservoir models to fit observed behavior, and methods for estimating uncertainty.
sources.quote: Obtaining even a single history-matched reservoir model requires a substantial amount of effort, but the past decade has seen remarkable progress in the ability to generate reservoir simulation models that match large amounts of production data.
sources.cited_for: It explains the work involved in fitting past production and why that differs from predicting an unseen response.
sources.not_established: Matching observed production does not demonstrate prediction of a response withheld from model fitting and selection.

sources.who: Suresh Kumar Govindarajan and colleagues, IIT Madras
sources.showed: Their conceptual review identifies how flow models lose details of fluid boundaries and connected paths when translating behavior in tiny rock spaces to reservoir scale.
sources.quote: First, pore-scale interface geometry and topology are averaged out.
sources.cited_for: It explains physical details that reservoir forecasts need to represent despite simplifying the rock and fluids.
sources.not_established: The review offers no replacement flow model or demonstration of blind reservoir forecasting.

shown: Oliver and Chen describe progress in models that match observed production. Govindarajan and colleagues explain where simplified flow descriptions lose physical detail. Neither review demonstrates reliable field forecasts made without fitting the response being predicted.
missing: A transferable method must connect flow through tiny rock spaces to whole-reservoir forecasts without fitting the target production response.
The method must preserve the effects of connected flow paths and fluid boundaries while remaining practical to compute at reservoir scale.
Field tests must demonstrate useful forecast uncertainty and repeatable results across materially different reservoirs.

milestones.label: Forecasts fixed before the production response is seen
milestones.explanation: Forecasts of fluid arrival, oil output and ultimate recovery, plus the model and selection procedure, would have to be registered before the target response is seen. This would separate prediction from fitting.

milestones.label: Earlier production use clearly distinguished
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to distinguish forecasts calibrated with earlier production from forecasts using rock, fluid and reservoir measurements alone. These establish different prediction capabilities.

milestones.label: Success criteria and recovery endpoints fixed beforehand
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to predeclare operations, starting assumptions, uncertainty, decision-relevant error limits and a recovery endpoint. This would make success meaningful, with recovery validation incomplete until that endpoint is observed.

milestones.label: Repeatable forecasts across different reservoir types
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat forecasts across different reservoirs, including carbonate, a reservoir rock type, with failures, input sensitivity and computing needs reported. This would establish the tested range.

uncertain: How much forecast error would leave a development decision unchanged, and which recovery endpoint should count as success?
How reliably can errors in the flow description be separated from errors in measured reservoir structure, starting conditions and operations?
How widely would successful forecasts transfer beyond the reservoir types and flow conditions tested?

page.title: Blind prediction of multiphase reservoir flow
page.definition: A model predicts reservoir oil, water and gas flow from pore geometry, fluid properties, wettability (which fluid preferentially contacts rock) and reservoir measurements, without fitting field production. Forecasts fixed before disclosure of the predicted response include breakthrough (injected fluid reaching a producer), oil rates, recovery to a specified endpoint and uncertainty.

goal.need: The recovery ranges below quantify the motivation for understanding displacement and sweep. The 2014 review relates oil recovery to pore-scale displacement, reservoir connectivity, sweep and operating limits. Reservoir simulation supports comparisons of development plans; history matching estimates model variables from observed reservoir behavior. The predictive goal is to make those comparisons before field production supplies calibration data.

completion.title: An independent team validates blind pore-derived forecasts in a different petroleum reservoir.
completion.criterion: An independent team reproduces blind field validation of the same pore-derived flow method in a different reservoir. Before production is disclosed, the model predicts injected-fluid breakthrough, oil-rate history and cumulative oil recovery to an explicitly defined, subsequently observed endpoint, using measured rock, fluid and reservoir inputs without field-production calibration or model selection against production. Observations satisfy error and uncertainty limits fixed before disclosure by the field-test protocol, with uncertainty small enough to preserve its stated development choice. These are Atlas-proposed conditions.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body was found to have defined this complete test.
completion.basis: Searched DOE subsurface roadmaps, SPE comparative-solution benchmarks, PRMS guidance and blind field-prediction papers for a completion test excluding production calibration; none was found. PRMS permits earlier history matching and specifies qualitative agreement over 6–12 withheld months. Independent transfer, observed recovery and decision-specific acceptance limits are Atlas fallback conditions.

milestones.title: Two-phase relative permeability is predicted from pore geometry without adjustable parameters.
milestones.criterion: Predict two-phase relative permeability, each fluid's mobility relative to single-phase flow, from specified granular pore geometry without adjustable parameters or supplementary pore-structure measurements. Bryant and Blunt reported comparison with measurements on sand packs, bead packs and a simple sandstone on 1 August 1992. Their accessible abstract supplies neither experimental sample counts nor a numerical acceptance tolerance. This establishes a laboratory comparison without prospective blinding.
milestones.set_by: BP Research Centre; Bryant and Blunt's published experimental-comparison protocol, restricted to simple granular media and sandstone. It specifies no numerical agreement tolerance.
milestones.threshold_quote: Because the microstructure is known, the calculations do not involve any adjustable parameters or supplementary measurements of pore structure.

milestones.title: A pore-network model predicts two-phase relative permeability across three wetting regimes.
milestones.criterion: After matching capillary pressure and measured wettability, predict relative permeability for water-, oil- and mixed-wet media without further model adjustment. On 15 July 2004, Valvatne and Blunt reported laboratory comparisons using one 27 mm³ Berea network containing 12,349 pores and 26,146 throats. Their oil-wet sandstone comparison used two cores with permeabilities of 248 and 328 mD. The study specifies no numerical passing tolerance and was not a prospective blind test.
milestones.set_by: Valvatne and Blunt, Imperial College London; published laboratory-validation protocol for sand packs and sandstones, rather than an industry acceptance standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: Then predictions of single and multiphase properties are made with no further adjustment of the model.

milestones.title: A reservoir model reasonably matches 6–12 months of withheld production rates or pressures.
milestones.criterion: Withhold the latest 6–12 months from history matching; predicted rates or pressures must reasonably match that interval under pressure or maximum-rate well control. PRMS supplies no numerical error tolerance. Related evidence from 2025 covers seven refractured wells in four datasets, calibrated before refracturing: mean mismatch in one-year cumulative-oil-production uplift was reported as 3.7%. Uplift uses an estimated no-refracturing baseline; one dataset extrapolated seven months to one year. The conference paper was not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Society of Petroleum Engineers and PRMS co-sponsoring societies; 2022 application guidelines, Chapter 6, Section 6.4.3. Earlier production calibration is permitted.
milestones.threshold_quote: reasonably match the data from the blind-test period.

milestones.title: A pore-derived model validates a blind forecast through an observed recovery endpoint in one reservoir.
milestones.criterion: In one petroleum reservoir, a model derived from pore geometry, wettability and fluid measurements predicts injected-fluid breakthrough, oil-rate history and cumulative recovery through a subsequently observed endpoint. No field-production response is used for calibration or model selection. Observations satisfy error and uncertainty limits fixed before disclosure by the field-test protocol, with uncertainty small enough to preserve its stated development choice. This is an Atlas-proposed field-demonstration test.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of DOE roadmaps, PRMS guidance and published blind field studies found no acceptance test for this production-uncalibrated demonstration.

not_found: No external completion test specifying forecast-error limits, reservoir coverage and an observed recovery endpoint was found for production-uncalibrated pore-to-field prediction.
No independently replicated field demonstration satisfying the proposed completion test was located.
The 1992 paper's full text and experimental sample counts were unavailable through the opened abstract.
The supplied Darcy review could not be opened at its DOI or publisher page.
SPE-hosted PRMS pages were inaccessible; the guidelines were read in a Scribd-hosted copy.

results.finding: Two-phase relative permeability predicted without adjustable parameters; sample count and numerical agreement not reported.
results.detail: Compared with previously measured values for sand packs, bead packs and a simple sandstone. The abstract gives no acceptance tolerance; the comparison was not prospectively blinded.
results.quote: Because the microstructure is known, the calculations do not involve any adjustable parameters or supplementary measurements of pore structure. The computed relative permeabilities are successfully compared with experimental values previously measured on sand packs, bead packs, and a simple sandstone.

results.finding: For two reservoir rocks, blind pore-network predictions showed water relative-permeability discrepancies below Sw = 0.3.
results.detail: The model was anchored to capillary-pressure data and tested on a mixed-wet sandstone and an oil-wet carbonate. It did not demonstrate predictions across all three required wetting regimes.
results.quote:
As for sample
SS4, the simulated water relative permeability curve displays clear percolation threshold
effects at low water saturations (  Sw < 0.3 ).

results.finding: For seven refractured wells, the mean mismatch in predicted one-year cumulative oil-production uplift was 3.7%.
results.detail: Models were calibrated before reviewing post-refracturing production. Uplift depends on an estimated no-refracturing baseline and is not a direct rate or pressure error; one dataset was extrapolated from seven months. The stated well-control condition is not established for all forecasts.
results.quote: The average mismatch in predicted uplift between the simulations and actual was 3.7%.
